Azilsartan Medoxomil: Azilsartan is metabolized into two primary metabolites. The major metabolite in plasma, referred to as metabolite M-II, is formed via O-dealkylation. The minor metabolite, referred to as metabolite M-I, is formed through decarboxylation. Systemic exposures to the major and minor metabolites in humans are approximately 50% and less than 1% of azilsartan, respectively. Neither M-I nor M-II contributes to the pharmacologic activity of azilsartan medoxomil. The primary enzyme responsible for azilsartan metabolism is CYP2C9. Following an oral dose of radiolabeled azilsartan medoxomil, approximately 55% of the radioactivity is recovered in feces and 42% in urine, with 15% of the dose excreted in urine as unchanged azilsartan. Steady-state levels of azilsartan are achieved within five days, and no accumulation occurs in plasma with repeated once-daily dosing. Chlorthalidone: The majority of chlorthalidone is excreted unchanged by the kidneys. Nonrenal routes of elimination have not yet been clarified. Data are unavailable regarding the percentage of the dose excreted as unchanged drug and metabolites, the concentration of the drug in body fluids, the degree of uptake by specific organs or the fetus, or its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier. Pharmacokinetics of Azilsartan Medoxomil: The effects of demographic and functional factors on the pharmacokinetics of azilsartan were studied in singleand multiple-dose studies. Pharmacokinetic measures indicating the magnitude of these effects are presented as changes relative to a reference (test/reference). Nonclinical Toxicology: No carcinogenicity, mutagenicity, or fertility studies have been conducted with the combination of azilsartan medoxomil and chlorthalidone. However, such studies have been conducted for azilsartan medoxomil alone. In carcinogenicity studies, the highest doses tested (450 mg/kg/day in mice and 600 mg/kg/day in rats) produced exposures to azilsartan that were 12 times (in mice) and 27 times (in rats) the average human exposure at the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) of 80 mg/day. For metabolite M-II, the highest doses tested (approximately 8000 mg/kg/day in male mice, 11,000 mg/kg/day in female mice, 1000 mg/kg/day in male rats, and up to 3000 mg/kg/day in female rats) produced exposures approximately 30 times (in mice) and 7 times (in rats) the average human exposure to M-II at the MRHD. Mutagenesis: Azilsartan medoxomil, azilsartan, and M-II were positive for structural chromosomal aberrations in the Chinese Hamster Lung Cytogenic Assay. Structural chromosomal aberrations were observed with azilsartan medoxomil without metabolic activation. Azilsartan was also positive in this assay both with and without metabolic activation. The major human metabolite, M-II, was positive in this assay during a 24-hour test without metabolic activation. However, azilsartan medoxomil, azilsartan, and M-II were negative for genotoxic potential in the Ames reverse mutation assay (using Salmonella typhimurium and Escherichia coli), the in vitro Chinese Hamster Ovary Cell forward mutation assay, the in vitro mouse lymphoma (tk) gene mutation test, the ex vivo unscheduled DNA synthesis test, and the in vivo mouse and/or rat bone marrow micronucleus assay. Impairment of Fertility: Azilsartan medoxomil had no effect on the fertility of male or female rats at oral doses up to 1000 mg/kg/day. Fertility was also unaffected at doses up to 3000 mg/kg/day of M-II. Edarbyclor: The safety profiles of azilsartan medoxomil and chlorthalidone monotherapy have been individually established. To characterize the toxicological profile of Edarbyclor, a 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study was conducted in rats. The results indicated that the combined administration of azilsartan medoxomil, M-II, and chlorthalidone resulted in increased exposures to chlorthalidone. Pharmacologically mediated toxicity, including suppression of body weight gain and decreased food consumption in male rats, as well as increases in blood urea nitrogen in both sexes, was enhanced by coadministration of azilsartan medoxomil, M-II, and chlorthalidone. Aside from these findings, no toxicologically synergistic effects were observed in this study. Embryo-Fetal Development: In an embryo-fetal developmental study in rats, there was no evidence of teratogenicity or increased fetal mortality in the litters of dams receiving azilsartan medoxomil, M-II, and chlorthalidone concomitantly at maternally toxic doses.
